title: IV. Rebellion
paragraphs: "I have to make you a confession," Ivan began. "I've never been able to understand how one is supposed to love one's neighbor. It's precisely one's neighbors, to my mind, that are impossible to love—though one might manage to love people from a distance. I once read somewhere about a saint, John the Merciful, that when a hungry, frozen beggar came to him, he took the man into his own bed, held him in his arms, and began breathing into his mouth, which was foul and putrid from some horrible disease. I'm convinced he did that out of 'self-laceration,' out of the self-laceration of falseness, for the sake of a charity imposed as duty, as a penance laid on himself. For anyone to love another person, that person has to stay hidden, because the moment he shows his face, the love vanishes."

"Father Zossima has said something like that more than once," Alyosha observed. "He too said that a man's face often keeps people who aren't practiced in love from loving him. And yet there's a great deal of love in mankind, love that's almost Christlike. I know that myself, Ivan."

"Well, I know nothing of it so far, and I can't understand it, and the vast bulk of mankind is right there with me. The question is whether that's down to men's bad qualities or whether it's simply built into their nature. To my mind, Christlike love for one's fellow man is a miracle impossible here on earth. He was God. We are not gods. Suppose, for instance, that I suffer intensely. No one else can ever know exactly how much I suffer, because he is someone else, not me. And what's more, a man is rarely willing to admit another person's suffering, as though it were some kind of distinction. Why won't he admit it, do you think? Because I smell unpleasant, because I've got a stupid face, because I once stepped on his foot. Besides, there's suffering and there's suffering; degrading, humiliating suffering, the kind that humbles me—hunger, say—my benefactor might allow for that; but when you get to a higher kind of suffering—suffering for an idea, say—he'll rarely admit that at all, maybe because my face doesn't match what he imagines a man suffering for an idea ought to look like. And so he strips me of his favor on the spot, and not out of any real malice. Beggars, especially genteel ones, ought never to show themselves in person, but should beg for charity through the newspapers instead. One can love one's neighbors in the abstract, or even from a distance, but up close it's almost impossible. If it were like on stage, in the ballet, where beggars come on wearing silk rags and tattered lace, begging for alms in graceful little dances, then one might enjoy watching them. But even then we wouldn't really love them. But enough of that. I only wanted to show you my point of view. I meant to talk about the suffering of humanity in general, but we'd better limit ourselves to the suffering of children. That cuts my argument down to a tenth of its scope, but we'd better stick to children, even though it weakens my case. But, first, children can be loved even up close, even when they're dirty, even when they're ugly—though I don't think children are ever really ugly. The second reason I won't talk about grown-ups is that, besides being repulsive and unworthy of love, they've got a kind of compensation—they've eaten the apple and know good and evil, they've become 'like gods.' And they go on eating it still. But children haven't eaten anything, and so far they're innocent. Do you love children, Alyosha? I know you do, and you'll understand why I'd rather talk about them. If they too suffer horribly on this earth, it must be for their fathers' sins, they must be punished on their fathers' behalf, for the fathers who ate the apple—but that kind of reasoning belongs to another world, and it's incomprehensible to the human heart here on earth. The innocent shouldn't suffer for someone else's sins, and especially not innocents like these! You might be surprised at me, Alyosha, but I'm terribly fond of children too. And notice this: cruel people, violent people, rapacious people, Karamazovs even, are often very fond of children. Children, while they're still quite small—up to seven, say—are so remote from grown-ups; they're practically a different species, as it were. I knew a criminal in prison who had, over the course of his career as a burglar, murdered whole families, children included. But once he was locked up, he developed a strange fondness for them. He spent all his time at his window watching the children play in the prison yard. He trained one little boy to come up to his window and became great friends with him.... You don't know why I'm telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches, and I'm sad."
"You have a strange way of talking," Alyosha observed uneasily, "as if you weren't quite yourself."

"By the way, a Bulgarian I met recently in Moscow," Ivan went on, as though he hadn't heard his brother's remark, "told me about the crimes the Turks and Circassians have been committing all over Bulgaria, out of fear of a general uprising of the Slavs. They burn villages, they murder, they violate women and children, they nail their prisoners' ears to the fences and leave them there until morning, and in the morning they hang them—all sorts of things you couldn't even imagine. People talk sometimes about 'bestial' cruelty, but that's a great injustice, an insult to the beasts; no animal could ever be as cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. A tiger only tears and gnaws, that's all it knows how to do. It would never think of nailing people's ears to anything, even if it could. Those Turks took real pleasure in torturing children too—cutting an unborn child out of its mother's womb, tossing babies into the air and catching them on the points of their bayonets, right in front of their mothers' eyes. Doing it in front of the mothers was what gave the whole thing its flavor. Here's another scene I found particularly striking. Picture a trembling mother holding her baby, surrounded by a ring of Turkish soldiers. They've dreamed up a little diversion: they pet the baby, they laugh to make it laugh. It works, the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk points a pistol four inches from the baby's face. The baby laughs with delight, reaches its little hands toward the pistol, and he pulls the trigger right in the baby's face and blows its brains out. Artistic, wasn't it? By the way, they say Turks are particularly fond of sweets."
"Brother, what are you getting at?" Alyosha asked.
"I think that if the devil doesn't exist, and man has invented him, then man has invented him in his own image and likeness."
"Just as he did with God, then?" Alyosha observed.

"'Tis wonderful how you can turn words, as Polonius says in Hamlet," Ivan laughed. "You're turning my own words against me. Well, I'm glad. Yours must be a fine God, if man created Him in his own image and likeness. You just asked what I was getting at. You see, I have a fondness for collecting certain facts—I even copy anecdotes of a certain kind out of newspapers and books, and would you believe, I've already put together quite a collection. The Turks, of course, are part of it, but they're foreigners. I've got homegrown specimens that are even better than the Turks. You know we favor beating here—rods and whips, that's our national tradition. Nailing ears is unthinkable for us, since we are, after all, Europeans. But the rod and the whip we've always had with us, and no one can take them away. Abroad these days they've mostly given up beating. Manners have grown more humane, or laws have been passed, so they no longer dare flog people. But they make up for it in another way, just as national in its own place as ours is here. So national, in fact, that it would be nearly impossible for us—though I think we're being inoculated with it, now that the religious movement has started up among our aristocracy. I have a charming pamphlet, translated from the French, describing the execution, quite recently, five years ago, of a murderer named Richard—a young man, I believe, twenty-three, who repented and converted to the Christian faith right there on the scaffold. This Richard was an illegitimate child, handed over by his parents at the age of six to some shepherds in the Swiss mountains. They raised him to work for them. He grew up among them like a little wild animal. The shepherds taught him nothing, barely fed or clothed him, and sent him out at seven to herd sheep in the cold and wet, and not one of them hesitated or felt a shred of scruple about treating him that way. Quite the opposite—they thought they had every right to, since Richard had been handed over to them like a piece of property, and they didn't even see the need to feed him. Richard himself describes how, during those years, like the Prodigal Son in the Gospel, he longed to eat the mash they fed the pigs, which were being fattened for sale. But they wouldn't even give him that, and beat him whenever he stole it from the pigs. That's how he spent his entire childhood and youth, until he grew up and was strong enough to run off and become a thief. This savage began earning his living as a day laborer in Geneva. He drank away his wages, lived like an animal, and ended up killing and robbing an old man. He was caught, tried, and sentenced to death. They're not sentimentalists over there. And in prison he was immediately surrounded by pastors, members of Christian brotherhoods, philanthropic ladies, and the like. They taught him to read and write in prison, expounded the Gospel to him. They exhorted him, worked on him, drummed at him without letup, until at last he solemnly confessed his crime. He was converted. He wrote to the court himself that he was a monster, but that in the end God had granted him light and shown him grace. All of Geneva was in an uproar over him—all philanthropic, religious Geneva. All the aristocratic, well-bred society of the town rushed to the prison, kissed Richard, embraced him: 'You are our brother, you have found grace.' And all Richard does is weep with emotion: 'Yes, I've found grace! All through my youth and childhood I was glad to get pigs' food, but now even I have found grace. I am dying in the Lord.' 'Yes, Richard, die in the Lord; you shed blood, and you must die. It's not your fault you didn't know the Lord, back when you coveted the pigs' food and were beaten for stealing it—which was very wrong of you, mind, since stealing is forbidden—but you shed blood, and you must die.' And on the last day, Richard, utterly limp, does nothing but weep and repeat over and over: 'This is the happiest day of my life. I am going to the Lord.' 'Yes,' cry the pastors and the judges and the philanthropic ladies. 'This is the happiest day of your life, for you are going to the Lord!' They all walk or ride in procession to the scaffold, behind the prison cart. At the scaffold they call out to Richard: 'Die, brother, die in the Lord, for even you have found grace!' And so, covered in his brothers' kisses, Richard is dragged up onto the scaffold and led to the guillotine. And they chop off his head in the most brotherly fashion, because he had found grace. Yes, that's very telling. That pamphlet was translated into Russian by some Russian philanthropists of aristocratic rank with evangelical leanings, and it's been distributed free of charge, for the enlightenment of the people. The Richard case is interesting because it's so national in its own way. Even though it strikes us as absurd to cut off a man's head just because he's become our brother and found grace, we've got our own specialty, which is arguably even worse. Our historical pastime is inflicting pain, straight up, for the sheer satisfaction of it. There are lines in Nekrasov describing a peasant lashing a horse across the eyes, 'across its meek eyes'—everyone must have seen it. It's peculiarly Russian. He describes a feeble little nag that's buckled under too heavy a load and can't move. The peasant beats it, beats it savagely, beats it at last without even knowing what he's doing, drunk on cruelty, thrashing it over and over without mercy. 'However weak you are, you'll pull it, even if it kills you.' The nag strains, and then he starts lashing the poor defenseless creature across its weeping, its 'meek eyes.' The frantic animal tugs and hauls the load, trembling all over, gasping for breath, lurching sideways in some unnatural, spasmodic motion—it's dreadful, in Nekrasov. But that's only a horse, and God gave us horses to be beaten. Or so the Tatars taught us, and left us the knout as a keepsake. But men can be beaten too. A well-educated, cultured gentleman and his wife once beat their own child with a birch rod—a girl of seven. I have the exact account of it. The father was pleased that the birch had plenty of twigs on it. 'It stings more,' he said, and set about stinging his daughter. I know for a fact there are people who, with every blow, work themselves into a kind of sensual pleasure, literal sensuality, that grows and grows with every blow they land. They beat the child for a minute, five minutes, ten minutes, harder and more savagely as they go. The child screams. Eventually the child can't scream anymore, just gasps, 'Daddy! Daddy!' By some diabolical, unseemly stroke of chance, the case ended up in court. A lawyer is hired. Russians have long called a defense lawyer 'a conscience for hire.' The lawyer protests in his client's defense: 'It's such a simple matter,' he says, 'an everyday domestic occurrence. A father disciplines his child. To our shame, it's ended up in court.' The jury, won over, returns a favorable verdict. The public roars with delight that the torturer has been acquitted. Ah, what a pity I wasn't there! I'd have proposed taking up a collection in his honor! Charming pictures.

"But I've got even better ones about children. I've collected a great, great deal about Russian children, Alyosha. There was a little girl of five whose own father and mother hated her—'most respectable, worthy people, well-educated and well-bred.' You see, I have to say it again: it's a peculiar trait in a lot of people, this love of torturing children, children specifically. Toward every other kind of person, these same torturers behave gently, generously even, like proper cultivated, humane Europeans; but they're very fond of tormenting children—fond, even, of the children themselves, in that particular sense. It's precisely the child's helplessness that tempts the tormentor, precisely the angelic trust of a child who has no refuge and no appeal, that sets his vile blood boiling. In every man, of course, there's a demon hidden away—the demon of rage, the demon of lustful heat at the screams of a tortured victim, the demon of lawlessness let off its chain, the demon of the diseases that come with vice—gout, kidney trouble, and so on.

"This poor five-year-old was subjected to every torture imaginable by those cultivated parents. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason at all until her whole body was one bruise. Then they moved on to still finer refinements of cruelty—locked her up all night, in the cold and frost, in an outhouse, and because she didn't ask to be let out at night (as if a five-year-old, sunk in her angelic, deep sleep, could somehow be trained to wake up and ask), they smeared her face with excrement and forced it into her mouth—and it was her mother, her own mother, who did this. And that mother could sleep at night, hearing the poor child's groans! Can you understand why a small creature, who can't even grasp what's being done to her, would beat her aching little chest with her tiny fist, alone in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, uncomplaining tears to 'dear, kind God' to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend, my brother, you pious, humble little novice? Do you understand why this outrage has to happen, and is allowed to happen? Without it, I'm told, man couldn't have existed on earth at all, because he couldn't have known good and evil. Why should he need to know that devilish good and evil, when it costs so much? Why, the entire world of knowledge isn't worth that one child's prayer to 'dear, kind God'! I say nothing about the sufferings of grown-ups—they ate the apple, damn them, and the devil take the lot of them! But these little ones! I'm making you suffer, Alyosha, you're not yourself. I'll stop if you want."
"Never mind. I want to suffer too," Alyosha murmured.

"One picture, just one more, because it's so striking, so telling, and I only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities—I've forgotten the title, I must look it up. This was in the darkest days of serfdom, at the beginning of the century—and long live the Liberator of the People! In those days there was a general, well connected among the aristocracy, the owner of vast estates, one of those men—somewhat exceptional, I believe, even for that time—who, retiring from service into a life of leisure, become convinced they've earned absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were men like that back then. So our general, settled on his estate of two thousand souls, lives in splendor, lording it over his poor neighbors as though they were dependents put on earth to amuse him. He keeps kennels with hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys—all mounted, all in uniform. One day a serf boy, a small child of eight, threw a stone while playing and hurt the paw of the general's favorite hound. 'Why is my favorite dog limping?' He's told that the boy threw a stone and hurt the dog's paw. 'So it was you.' The general looks the child up and down. 'Take him.' The boy is taken—taken from his mother and locked up overnight. Early the next morning the general rides out on horseback with the hounds, his dependents, his dog-boys and huntsmen, all mounted around him in full hunting dress. The household servants are summoned to witness, for their own edification, and standing in front of them all is the child's mother. The boy is brought out from the lockup. It's a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day, a perfect day for a hunt. The general orders the child stripped; the boy is stripped bare. He shivers, numb with terror, not even daring to cry.... 'Make him run,' the general commands. 'Run! Run!' the dog-boys shout. The boy runs.... 'Sic him!' the general bellows, and he sets the entire pack of hounds on the child. The hounds catch him and tear him to pieces before his mother's eyes!... I believe the general was later declared unfit to manage his own estates. Well—what did he deserve? To be shot? Shot, for the satisfaction of our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!"
"To be shot," Alyosha murmured, lifting his eyes to Ivan with a pale, twisted smile.
"Bravo!" Ivan cried, delighted. "If even you say so.... What a fine monk you are! So there's a little devil sitting in your heart too, Alyosha Karamazov!"
"What I said was absurd, but—"

"That's exactly the point, that 'but'!" Ivan cried. "Let me tell you, novice, the absurd is one of the most necessary things on earth. The world rests on absurdities, and maybe nothing would ever have happened in it without them. We know what we know!"
"What do you know?"

"I understand nothing," Ivan went on, as though in delirium. "I don't want to understand anything anymore. I want to stick to the fact. I made up my mind long ago not to understand. If I try to understand anything, I'll betray the fact, and I've resolved to stick to the fact."
"Why are you testing me like this?" Alyosha cried, suddenly distressed. "Will you finally say what you mean?"
"Of course I will; that's exactly what I've been building up to. You're dear to me, I don't want to let you go, and I won't hand you over to your Zossima."
Ivan fell silent for a moment, and his face suddenly turned very sad.

"Listen! I only took the case of children to make my argument clearer. I'll say nothing about the rest of humanity's tears, which soak the earth from its crust to its core. I've deliberately narrowed my subject. I'm a bug, and I admit, in all humility, that I can't understand why the world is arranged the way it is. Men are to blame for it themselves, I suppose; they were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven knowing perfectly well they'd become unhappy for it, so there's no need to pity them. With my pitiful, earthbound, Euclidean understanding, all I know is that there's suffering, and that no one is guilty; that cause follows effect, simply and directly; that everything flows and finds its own level—but that's just Euclidean nonsense, I know that much, and I can't bring myself to live by it! What good does it do me that no one is guilty and that cause follows effect simply and directly, and that I understand that perfectly well? I need justice, or I'll destroy myself. And not justice somewhere off in infinite time and space, but here, on earth, justice I could see with my own eyes. I've believed in it. I want to see it for myself, and if I'm already dead by then, let me rise again, because if it all happens without me, it'll be too unfair. Surely I haven't suffered simply so that I, my crimes and my sufferings, could go to fertilize the soil for someone else's future harmony. I want to see, with my own eyes, the doe lie down with the lion, and the murdered man rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. All the religions of the world are built on that longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I supposed to do about them? That's a question I can't answer. For the hundredth time, I repeat, there are countless questions, but I've only taken up the children, because in their case, what I mean is so unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone has to suffer to pay for the eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it, tell me, please? It's utterly incomprehensible why they should have to suffer, why they should have to pay for that harmony. Why should they too have to serve as raw material to enrich the soil for some future harmony? I understand solidarity in sin among adults. I understand solidarity in punishment too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it's really true that they have to share responsibility for all their fathers' crimes, then that kind of truth doesn't belong to this world, and it's beyond my comprehension. Some wit might say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned eventually anyway, but you see, he didn't grow up—he was torn to pieces by dogs at the age of eight. Oh, Alyosha, I'm not blaspheming! I understand, of course, what an upheaval of the whole universe it will be, when everything in heaven and on earth blends into one great hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has ever lived cries out: 'Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed.' When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three of them cry out through their tears, 'Thou art just, O Lord!'—then, of course, the crown of all knowledge will be reached, and everything will be made clear. But what stops me cold, right here, is that I can't accept that harmony. And while I'm still on this earth, I hurry to take my own precautions. You see, Alyosha, it may very well happen that if I live to see that moment, or rise again to witness it, I too might cry out with all the rest, watching the mother embrace her child's torturer: 'Thou art just, O Lord!'—but I don't want to cry that out then. While there's still time, I hasten to protect myself now, and so I renounce that higher harmony altogether. It isn't worth the tears of that one tortured child who beat her aching chest with her little fist and prayed in her filthy outhouse, with her unavenged tears, to 'dear, kind God'! It isn't worth it, because those tears remain unatoned for. They have to be atoned for, or there can be no harmony at all. But how? How could you possibly atone for them? Is it even possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good could hell possibly do, once those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there's a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don't want any more suffering. And if the sufferings of children are meant to swell the total sum of suffering needed to purchase the truth, then I protest that the truth isn't worth such a price. I don't want the mother to embrace the man who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to, let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering inflicted on her as a mother. But she has no right to forgive him the suffering of her tortured child; she dare not forgive the torturer that, even if the child himself were to forgive him! And if that's so, if they dare not forgive, then what becomes of harmony? Is there anyone anywhere in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and who actually could forgive? I don't want harmony. Out of love for humanity, I don't want it. I would rather be left with suffering that goes unavenged. I would rather stay with my unavenged suffering and my unsatisfied indignation, even if I turn out to be wrong. Besides, the price being asked for harmony is too high; it's beyond our means to pay that much just to get in. And so I hurry to hand back my entrance ticket, and if I'm an honest man, I'm bound to hand it back as soon as I possibly can. And that's exactly what I'm doing. It's not God I don't accept, Alyosha—it's just that I most respectfully return Him the ticket."
"That's rebellion," Alyosha murmured, looking down.

"Rebellion? I'm sorry you'd call it that," Ivan said earnestly. "One can hardly live in a state of rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I'm putting it to you directly—answer me. Imagine that you're constructing the fabric of human destiny, with the ultimate goal of making people happy in the end, giving them peace and rest at last—but that to do it, it was essential, unavoidable, to torture just one tiny creature to death—that baby beating its chest with its little fist, say—and to build that whole edifice on her unavenged tears—would you agree to be the architect, on those terms? Tell me, and tell the truth."
"No, I wouldn't agree," Alyosha said softly.

"And can you accept the idea that the people you're building it for would actually agree to accept their happiness on the foundation of one small victim's unatoned-for blood? And having accepted it, remain happy forever after?"

"No, I can't accept that. Brother," Alyosha said suddenly, his eyes flashing, "you just asked whether there's anyone in the whole world who has the right to forgive, and who could forgive. But there is such a Being, and He can forgive everything, everyone, for everything, because He gave His own innocent blood for all of it, for everyone. You've forgotten Him, and it's on Him that the whole edifice is built, and it's to Him that they cry out, 'Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed!'"

"Ah! The One without sin, and His blood! No, I haven't forgotten Him—quite the opposite, I've been wondering this whole time why you hadn't brought Him up sooner, since usually every argument on your side puts Him front and center. Do you know, Alyosha—don't laugh!—I composed a poem about a year ago. If you can spare me another ten minutes, I'll tell it to you."
"You wrote a poem?"

"Oh, no, I didn't write it down," Ivan laughed, "and I've never written two lines of verse in my life. But I made up this poem in prose, and I remember it. I got carried away composing it. You'll be my first reader—that is, my first listener. Why should an author pass up even one listener?" Ivan smiled. "Shall I tell it to you?"
"I'm listening," said Alyosha.
"My poem is called 'The Grand Inquisitor'; it's a ridiculous thing, but I want to tell it to you."
